turns.message: What should I do if my tire is flat?
turns.answer:
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.

Common causes include a nail, screw or other object in the tread; a cut or bulge in the sidewall from a pothole or kerb; or a leaking valve.

Use the spare tire or repair kit as the owner's manual describes; a temporary spare has speed and distance limits. If the sidewall is damaged or you can't change it safely, call roadside assistance. In a rental car, contact the rental team first.

turns.message: How often should I check my tire pressure?
turns.answer:
Correct tire pressure and enough tread are essential for grip, braking and steering. Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold, using the figures on the door-jamb sticker or in the owner's manual.

Common causes include slow leaks from punctures or valves; temperature changes; or uneven wear from wrong pressure or misalignment.

Inflate to the vehicle's placard pressure, not the maximum printed on the tire. Check the tread-wear indicators and look for cuts, bulges or uneven wear. Rotate the tires at the interval in the owner's manual.

Replace a tire with a bulge, a deep cut, or tread worn down to the wear indicators.

turns.message: What tire pressure should my Toyota Vios have?
turns.answer:
Correct tire pressure and enough tread are essential for grip, braking and steering. Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold, using the figures on the door-jamb sticker or in the owner's manual.

Common causes include slow leaks from punctures or valves; temperature changes; or uneven wear from wrong pressure or misalignment.

Inflate to the vehicle's placard pressure, not the maximum printed on the tire. Check the tread-wear indicators and look for cuts, bulges or uneven wear.

Replace a tire with a bulge, a deep cut, or tread worn down to the wear indicators.

turns.message: My tire blew out on the highway
turns.answer:
If a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the car straight. Don't brake hard: ease off the accelerator, let the car slow down gradually, then steer to a safe place and stop.

Common causes include under-inflation and overheating; overloading; impact damage from a pothole or kerb; or old or worn tires.

Once stopped, turn on your hazard lights and fit the spare only if it's safe to do so; otherwise call roadside assistance.

turns.message: There's a bulge on the sidewall of my tire
turns.answer:
A bulge, bubble or deep cut in the sidewall means the tire's internal structure is damaged and it can burst. Don't drive on it: stop safely and fit the spare or call roadside assistance.

Common causes include hitting a pothole or kerb; driving on an under-inflated tire; or a cut from debris.

Sidewall damage can't be repaired safely; the tire needs replacing.

turns.message: Why are my tires wearing on the inside edge?
turns.answer:
Uneven wear has typical patterns: both edges worn usually means under-inflation, the centre worn means over-inflation, one edge worn usually means misalignment, and patchy or cupped wear points to suspension or balance problems.

Possible causes include incorrect tire pressure, wheel misalignment, worn suspension parts, unbalanced wheels or skipped tire rotations.

Check and correct the tire pressures.

Replace any tire worn down to its wear indicators or with exposed cords.

turns.message: What is tire rotation?
turns.answer:
Rotating the tires means moving them between positions so they wear evenly. Follow the interval and pattern in the owner's manual, because some tires and cars need a specific pattern.

Combine rotation with a pressure and tread check.

turns.message: What is wheel balancing?
turns.answer:
Wheel balancing evens out the weight around each wheel and tire so they spin smoothly. Unbalanced wheels usually cause vibration through the steering wheel at certain speeds.

Have the wheels balanced when fitting new tires, after a puncture repair, or if vibration appears.

turns.message: Why is my car overheating?
turns.answer:
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly.

Possible causes include low coolant or a coolant leak; a thermostat stuck closed; a radiator fan that isn't switching on; a failing water pump; or a blocked or damaged radiator.

Once the engine has fully cooled, check the coolant level in the reservoir.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: What if the coolant is full?
turns.answer: With the coolant level correct, the cooling fan, thermostat and water pump are the next things to check. Check whether the radiator fan runs when the engine gets hot or when the A/C is switched on.

turns.message: My temperature gauge is going up
turns.answer:
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly.

Common causes include low coolant or a coolant leak; a thermostat stuck closed; a radiator fan that isn't switching on; or a failing water pump.

Once the engine has fully cooled, check the coolant level in the reservoir. Check whether the radiator fan runs when the engine gets hot or when the A/C is switched on.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: Is it safe to keep driving?
turns.answer: No. Driving an overheating engine can quickly warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket. Stop, let it cool completely, and have it checked before driving on.

turns.message: My engine is misfiring
turns.answer:
A misfire means one or more cylinders isn't burning fuel properly, which causes shaking, a rough idle, hesitation or loss of power.

Common causes include worn spark plugs or a failing ignition coil; a clogged or leaking fuel injector; an air (vacuum) leak; or low fuel pressure.

Note when it happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether the check-engine light is on or flashing. Have the diagnostic codes read; a cylinder-specific code such as P0301 shows where to start.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the car loses power, slow down and stop somewhere safe; a severe misfire can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

turns.message: My check engine light is flashing
turns.answer:
A flashing (blinking) check-engine light usually means a severe misfire that can quickly overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

Common causes include a failed spark plug or ignition coil; a fuel-injector fault; an air leak; or low compression.

Have the codes read as soon as possible.

Reduce speed and load, stop in a safe place as soon as you can, and avoid continued driving until the vehicle is inspected or towed.

turns.message: The red oil pressure light came on while driving
turns.answer:
If the red oil-pressure light comes on while driving, stop safely and switch off the engine as soon as possible. Don't restart it until the oil level has been checked.

A red oil-pressure warning means the engine may not be getting enough oil pressure, which can damage it within minutes. Leaks and oil burning lower the oil level more gradually.

Common causes include a low oil level; an oil leak from a gasket, seal or the drain plug; a worn oil pump or blocked oil pickup; or a faulty oil-pressure sensor.

With the engine off and the car on level ground, check the oil level on the dipstick as the owner's manual describes. Look under the car for fresh oil drips and note any burning-oil smell.

turns.message: How do I check my engine oil?
turns.answer:
Check the oil with the car on level ground and the engine off, as the owner's manual describes: wait a few minutes, pull out the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in, then pull it out again and read the level between the marks.

If it's low, add a little at a time using the oil grade in the owner's manual, then recheck; don't overfill. Needing to top up often points to a leak or oil burning; have it checked.

If the red oil-pressure light comes on, stop the engine as soon as it's safe.

turns.message: How often should I change engine oil?
turns.answer:
Oil change intervals depend on the engine, the oil type and how the car is driven, so follow the schedule in the owner's manual or the car's oil-life monitor.

Use whichever comes first in the schedule: the distance or the time since the last change. Use the severe-service schedule if the car does many short trips, stop-and-go traffic, towing or dusty driving. Check the oil level regularly between changes.

turns.message: My engine is making a knocking noise
turns.answer:
Engine noises point to different problems depending on the sound: knocking or pinging when accelerating, ticking from the top of the engine, rattling at start-up, or squealing from a belt.

Common causes include a low oil level or low oil pressure (ticking or knocking); worn engine bearings (deep knocking); pre-ignition from fuel quality or carbon build-up (pinging when accelerating); or a worn timing chain or tensioner (rattle at start-up).

Check the engine oil level first. Note when the noise happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether it changes with engine speed.

A loud knock together with the oil-pressure light means switch the engine off as soon as it's safe.

turns.message: The engine cranks but won't start
turns.answer:
If the engine cranks normally but won't start, it usually isn't getting fuel, spark or enough air, or the immobiliser is blocking it.

Common causes include an empty tank or a faulty fuel gauge; a failed fuel pump or blocked fuel filter; an ignition fault; or an immobiliser or key problem (security light flashing).

Check the fuel level and whether a security or key warning light is flashing; try the spare key if there's a key warning. Don't crank for long periods; pause between attempts to protect the starter and battery.

turns.message: Blue smoke from my exhaust
turns.answer:
Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke means the engine is burning oil.

Common causes include worn piston rings or valve-stem seals; a leaking turbocharger seal; a blocked crankcase ventilation (PCV) system; or too much engine oil.

Check the oil level regularly and top up with the oil grade in the owner's manual. Have the engine inspected to find where the oil is getting in.

If the oil level drops quickly or the oil-pressure light comes on, stop driving.

turns.message: white smoke from exhaust
turns.answer:
Thin white vapour that clears once the engine warms up is usually just condensation. Thick white smoke that keeps coming, especially with a sweet smell, can mean coolant is burning in the engine; a failed head gasket is one possible cause.

Common causes include condensation on a cold start (normal), coolant entering the combustion chamber, a failed head gasket or a cracked cylinder head.

Check the coolant level with the engine cold. Watch the temperature gauge.

If the engine starts to overheat or the coolant level keeps dropping, stop driving and have it inspected.

turns.message: What does a timing belt do?
turns.answer:
A timing belt or chain keeps the engine's valves and pistons in step. If it slips or breaks, the engine stops and can be badly damaged.

Check the service records or owner's manual for when the timing belt is due; many belts have a fixed replacement interval, chains usually don't.

If the engine suddenly cuts out and won't restart, don't keep cranking it; have it towed and inspected.

turns.message: Car won't start, just clicking
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

Common causes include a discharged or worn-out battery; loose or corroded battery terminals; something draining the battery while parked; or a failing starter motor or relay.

Rapid clicking with dim lights usually points to a weak battery or poor connection; a single click with bright lights can point to the starter. With the engine off, check that the battery terminals are tight and free of corrosion.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: What does an alternator do?
turns.answer: The alternator supplies electrical power and charges the battery while the engine runs in vehicles equipped with one.

turns.message: The battery light came on while driving
turns.answer:
Drive only as far as a safe place nearby, then stop; the car can lose power and stall when the battery runs down. If the temperature gauge also rises, stop straight away, because the same belt may drive the water pump.

A battery or charging light while driving means the charging system has a fault, usually an alternator that isn't charging, so the car is running on battery power and may stop.

Common causes include a failing alternator; a broken or slipping drive belt; loose or corroded battery connections; or a wiring or fuse fault.

Switch off electrical loads you don't need, such as the A/C, radio and heated seats.

turns.message: My battery dies overnight
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

Common causes include a discharged or worn-out battery; loose or corroded battery terminals; something draining the battery while parked; or a failing starter motor or relay.

Rapid clicking with dim lights usually points to a weak battery or poor connection; a single click with bright lights can point to the starter. With the engine off, check that the battery terminals are tight and free of corrosion.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: My radio stopped working, could it be a blown fuse?
turns.answer:
If a fuse blows again straight away there's a short circuit: don't fit a bigger fuse, have the wiring checked.

When one electrical item stops working, such as a light, the radio, a power outlet or a window, a blown fuse is a common cause.

Common causes include a blown fuse; a faulty relay; a damaged wire or connector; or a failed component.

With the ignition off, find the right fuse using the diagram in the owner's manual and check whether the metal strip inside is broken. Replace it only with a fuse of the same rating.

turns.message: I smell burning plastic from the dashboard
turns.answer:
A burning plastic or electrical smell can mean overheating wiring or a short circuit, which can start a fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.

Common causes include overheating or shorted wiring; a failing blower motor or resistor (smell through the vents); oil or coolant dripping onto the hot exhaust; or a slipping clutch or a dragging brake (burning rubber or acrid smell).

If you see smoke or flames, move well away from the car and call emergency services. Don't open the bonnet if smoke is coming from under it. If there's no smoke, let the car cool down and have it inspected before driving it again.

turns.message: How do I take care of my car battery?
turns.answer:
Keep the battery terminals clean and tight and avoid leaving lights or accessories on with the engine off. Batteries wear out with age, so have the battery tested if starting becomes slower.

Short trips and long periods parked drain a battery; drive regularly or use a suitable maintainer. Replace the battery with the type and rating listed in the owner's manual.

turns.message: My brakes feel spongy
turns.answer:
A spongy or soft brake pedal usually means air in the brake lines, low brake fluid from a leak, or a failing master cylinder. It reduces braking power.

Common causes include air in the brake lines, a brake-fluid leak, old brake fluid that has absorbed moisture or a failing master cylinder.

With the engine off, check the brake-fluid level in the reservoir and look for wet patches near the wheels.

A soft or sinking brake pedal is safety-critical: stop safely as soon as you can and arrange a tow instead of driving to a workshop.

turns.message: My brakes are not working while driving
turns.answer:
If your brakes fail while driving, pump the brake pedal firmly, shift to a lower gear, and apply the parking brake gradually while steering to a safe place. Turn on your hazard lights and use the horn to warn others.

Common causes include a major brake-fluid leak, a failed master cylinder or overheated brakes on a long descent (brake fade).

Once stopped, don't drive the car again; have it towed for inspection.

turns.message: my brakes are squeaking when I stop
turns.answer:
A squeak or squeal when braking is usually caused by the pads and rotors: worn pads touching their wear indicator, moisture or light rust, brake dust, or glazed friction surfaces.

Common causes include pads worn down to the wear indicator; moisture or light surface rust, often in the morning or after rain; brake dust or debris between pad and rotor; or glazed pads or rotors.

A brief squeak on the first few stops in damp weather that then goes away is usually moisture. A squeal that is constant or getting louder should be inspected soon.

Grinding or a metal-on-metal sound usually means the pads are worn through; stop driving when it's safe and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: grinding noise when I brake
turns.answer:
A grinding or metal-on-metal noise when braking usually means the pads are worn through and metal is rubbing the rotor, or something is caught in the brake.

Common causes include pads worn down to the backing plate; a stone or debris caught between the rotor and its shield; a badly worn or damaged rotor; or a seized caliper.

Avoid hard braking and arrange a brake inspection straight away.

Grinding brakes can lose stopping power and quickly damage the rotors: stop using the car and have it inspected or towed.

turns.message: What does the ABS light mean?
turns.answer:
The ABS light means the anti-lock system has a fault. Normal braking usually still works, but the wheels can lock under hard braking. A red brake warning is more serious and can mean low brake fluid or a hydraulic problem.

Check the owner's manual for the exact warning symbol and what it advises.

If the red brake warning is on, the pedal feels soft or the car stops poorly, pull over safely and don't drive further; arrange a tow.

turns.message: When should brake fluid be changed?
turns.answer:
Brake fluid transmits the pedal pressure to the brakes. It absorbs moisture over time, so it's replaced at the interval in the owner's manual. A slowly dropping level can be pad wear; a fast drop means a leak.

Check the level against the marks on the reservoir with the engine off. Use only the brake-fluid type printed on the reservoir cap or in the owner's manual.

If the level drops quickly or the red brake warning comes on, don't drive the car; have the brakes checked.

turns.message: Car shakes when braking.
turns.answer:
Shaking or a pulsing pedal when braking usually means the brake rotors are uneven (often called warped), or there's a problem with the wheels, tires or suspension.

Common causes include uneven rotor thickness or deposits on the rotors; a sticking caliper; loose wheel nuts or wheel imbalance; or worn suspension parts.

Note whether you feel it through the pedal or the steering wheel, and at what speed. Have the rotors measured during a brake inspection.

If the vibration is severe or braking feels weaker, stop driving and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: What do brake pads do?
turns.answer: Brake pads press against a rotor or drum to create friction and slow the wheel. Rotors or drums provide the friction surface; calipers apply pad force in many disc-brake systems.

turns.message: Transmission slipping
turns.answer:
Transmission slipping is when the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up as it should, or gears engage late or harshly.

Common causes include low or worn-out transmission fluid; a fluid leak; worn clutches or bands inside the transmission; or a faulty solenoid, sensor or control module.

Note when it slips (cold, hot, a particular gear) and whether a transmission warning light is on. Look for red or brown fluid under the car.

If the car loses drive, the transmission smells burnt or an over-temperature warning appears, stop safely; continuing can cause major damage.

turns.message: How do I check transmission fluid?
turns.answer:
Transmission fluid lubricates, cools and operates the gearbox. Check and change it only as the owner's manual specifies; many modern automatics have no dipstick and need a workshop procedure.

Look for red or brown drips under the car. Very dark or burnt-smelling fluid should be checked by a technician.

turns.message: How many liters of transmission fluid does my car need?
turns.answer:
Transmission fluid lubricates, cools and operates the gearbox. Check and change it only as the owner's manual specifies; many modern automatics have no dipstick and need a workshop procedure.

Look for red or brown drips under the car. Very dark or burnt-smelling fluid should be checked by a technician.

turns.message: It's hard to shift gears in my manual car
turns.answer:
Difficulty selecting gears in a manual car usually comes from a clutch that isn't fully disengaging, low clutch fluid, worn synchronisers or a linkage problem.

Common causes include a clutch that doesn't fully disengage; low or leaking clutch hydraulic fluid; worn synchronisers (grinding when shifting); or a worn or misadjusted gear linkage.

Check that the clutch pedal goes fully down and comes back up normally. If the car has a clutch-fluid reservoir (often shared with the brake fluid), check its level.

If you can't select a gear or the clutch pedal stays down, stop and arrange assistance.

turns.message: My transmission is whining
turns.answer:
Whining, humming or clunking from the transmission can come from low fluid, worn bearings or gears, worn mounts or driveline parts.

Common causes include low or worn transmission fluid; worn bearings or gears; worn transmission or engine mounts; or worn CV joints or universal joints.

Note whether the noise changes with road speed, engine speed or when shifting. Look for fluid leaks under the car.

turns.message: My steering is heavy
turns.answer:
Steering that suddenly becomes heavy usually means power-steering assistance has been reduced or lost, or a front tire is low.

Common causes include a low or flat front tire; low power-steering fluid or a leak (hydraulic systems); a slipping or broken drive belt; or an electric power-steering fault, often with a warning light.

Check the front tire pressures and look for a flat. Look for a steering warning light on the dashboard.

If steering becomes hard while driving, slow down, hold the wheel firmly and stop somewhere safe. Don't continue if steering is difficult or unpredictable.

turns.message: I lost steering while driving
turns.answer:
After a steering failure while driving, don't drive the car again until it has been inspected; arrange a tow.

If you lose steering control while driving, stay calm, hold the wheel, turn on the hazard lights, ease off the accelerator and brake gently and steadily to stop. Don't brake hard or swerve.

Common causes include loss of power-steering assistance; a broken steering joint or linkage; or a seized or locked steering column.

If the car is parked and the wheel won't turn with the key, the steering lock is probably engaged: turn the wheel gently left and right while turning the key or pressing the start button.

turns.message: My steering wheel is locked and the key won't turn
turns.answer:
If you lose steering control while driving, stay calm, hold the wheel, turn on the hazard lights, ease off the accelerator and brake gently and steadily to stop. Don't brake hard or swerve.

Common causes include loss of power-steering assistance; a broken steering joint or linkage; or a seized or locked steering column.

If the car is parked and the wheel won't turn with the key, the steering lock is probably engaged: turn the wheel gently left and right while turning the key or pressing the start button.

After a steering failure while driving, don't drive the car again until it has been inspected; arrange a tow.

turns.message: My car keeps bouncing after bumps
turns.answer:
Worn shock absorbers or struts make the car keep bouncing after bumps, dive when braking and lean more in corners, and they can lengthen stopping distances.

Common causes include worn or leaking shock absorbers or struts; a broken spring; or worn mounts or bushings.

Look for oil leaking down the shock absorber body. Check the tires for uneven, scalloped wear.

turns.message: My steering wheel is not straight when driving straight
turns.answer:
Wheel alignment sets the angles of the wheels. Signs it's off include pulling to one side, a crooked steering wheel when driving straight, and uneven tire wear.

Common causes include hitting a pothole or kerb; worn steering or suspension parts; or suspension work without an alignment afterwards.

Check the tire pressures first, because uneven pressure can feel like misalignment. Have the alignment checked after a hard impact or when fitting new tires.

turns.message: Car pulls to the left.
turns.answer:
A car that pulls or drifts to one side usually has uneven tire pressure, wheel misalignment, a dragging brake or a worn steering or suspension part.

Common causes include uneven or low tire pressure; wheel misalignment; a sticking brake caliper; or uneven tire wear.

Check and correct the tire pressures first. Note whether it pulls all the time or only when braking; pulling only when braking points to the brakes.

If the pull is sudden or strong, or happens when braking, have it inspected before driving further.

turns.message: My steering wheel shakes at high speed
turns.answer:
A steering wheel that shakes at higher speeds is most often caused by unbalanced wheels, and sometimes by a damaged tire, a bent wheel or worn steering parts.

Common causes include unbalanced wheels; a tire with a bulge or uneven wear; a bent wheel; or worn tie-rod ends or suspension parts.

Have the wheels balanced and the tires checked for bulges. Make sure the wheel nuts are tight.

If the vibration is sudden or severe, slow down and stop safely; a tire may be failing.

turns.message: Clicking noise when turning
turns.answer:
A clicking or popping noise when turning is most often a worn outer CV joint on a front-wheel-drive car, usually after its rubber boot has torn.

Common causes include a worn CV joint; a torn CV boot that let grease out and dirt in; or worn suspension or steering parts.

With the engine off, look behind the front wheels for a torn boot or grease sprayed around. Have it inspected soon; a worn CV joint can break and cause loss of drive.

turns.message: My car suddenly started shaking violently
turns.answer:
Sudden, severe shaking can mean a tire is failing, a wheel is loose, or there's a serious engine or drivetrain fault. Slow down gradually and stop somewhere safe.

Common causes include a damaged or separating tire; loose wheel nuts; a severe engine misfire; or a broken engine mount or driveshaft.

Once stopped, look at the tires for bulges or damage and check whether the check-engine light is flashing. Don't continue until the cause is found; arrange an inspection or a tow.

turns.message: Whining noise when turning the steering wheel
turns.answer:
A whining or groaning noise when turning the wheel on a car with hydraulic power steering often means low power-steering fluid or a worn pump.

Common causes include low power-steering fluid or a leak; a worn power-steering pump; or a slipping drive belt.

With the engine off, check the power-steering fluid level if the car has a reservoir, using the fluid type in the owner's manual. Look for fluid leaks near the steering rack and pump.

If the steering also becomes heavy, drive carefully to a safe place and have it inspected.

turns.message: I smell gasoline near the car
turns.answer:
A strong fuel smell or a fuel leak is a fire risk. Don't start or keep running the engine, keep away from ignition sources such as sparks, flames and cigarettes, and move away from the car.

Common causes include a leaking fuel line, hose or injector seal; a damaged fuel tank; a loose or faulty fuel cap; or a fault in the fuel-vapour (EVAP) system.

If the smell is faint and only right after refuelling, check that the fuel cap is closed properly. For a strong or lasting smell, or any dripping fuel, have the car towed for inspection instead of driving it.

turns.message: There is smoke coming from under the hood
turns.answer:
Smoke from under the bonnet can be steam from overheating coolant, oil burning on hot parts, or an electrical fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.

Common causes include overheating and coolant boiling (white, sweet-smelling steam); oil leaking onto the hot exhaust (blue-grey smoke, burnt-oil smell); or an electrical fault (acrid smell of burning plastic).

Don't open the bonnet while smoke is coming out; opening it can feed a fire. If there are flames or the smoke keeps increasing, move well away from the car and call emergency services.

turns.message: Can I open the high-voltage battery pack?
turns.answer:
Hybrid and electric cars use high-voltage systems that can cause a fatal electric shock. Never open, touch or cut the orange high-voltage cables or the battery pack.

Leave high-voltage work to technicians trained and equipped for it. Follow the owner's manual for warnings, charging and towing.

After a crash, or if you see smoke, smell burning or hear hissing from the battery, move away from the vehicle and call emergency services.

turns.message: What coolant should I use?
turns.answer:
Coolant protects the engine from overheating, freezing and corrosion. Check the level in the reservoir with the engine cold, and replace it at the interval in the owner's manual using the specified coolant type.

Top up only with the coolant type in the owner's manual; don't mix types unless it allows it. A level that keeps dropping points to a leak; have it checked.

Never open the radiator or reservoir cap on a hot engine.

turns.message: When should I service my car?
turns.answer:
Maintenance schedules are based on both distance and time, whichever comes first. If a service is overdue, book it soon and check whether safety items such as brakes or tires were due.

Compare the odometer and the date of the last service with the schedule in the owner's manual. Don't skip safety-related items: brakes, tires, steering and fluid checks.

turns.message: When do I replace the air filter?
turns.answer:
Air, cabin and fuel filters, spark plugs and other wear items are replaced at intervals set by the vehicle maker, by distance or time.

Follow the maintenance schedule in the owner's manual or service booklet. Replace the engine air filter sooner if you drive in dusty conditions.

turns.message: My aircon is blowing warm air
turns.answer:
Weak or warm air from the A/C usually comes from low refrigerant, a compressor problem, a blocked cabin filter or condenser, or a blower or control fault.

Common causes include low refrigerant from a leak; a compressor or compressor-clutch fault; a clogged cabin air filter; or a blocked condenser or a condenser fan that isn't running.

Check whether air is blowing strongly; weak airflow points to the blower or cabin filter rather than the refrigerant. Check whether the fan in front of the radiator runs when the A/C is on.

turns.message: What is P0420?
turns.answer:
P0420: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1. Common causes: catalyst aged or poisoned (oil consumption, silicone, coolant); catalyst overheated by misfire or rich running; rear oxygen sensor sluggish, dirty or unsuitable. Typical signs: check engine light on, otherwise often no change in driving; emission test failed (higher HC, CO, NOx). This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: What does code P0300 mean?
turns.answer:
P0300: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected. Common causes: false air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket); worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils; fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel. Typical signs: check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate; rough idle, jerking, vibration. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light. Reduced-power (limp) mode is possible.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

P0171: System Too Lean Bank 1. Common causes: air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line); crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick); air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air). Typical signs: check engine light on (after two drive cycles); rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: What is P0300?
turns.answer:
P0300: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected. Common causes: false air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket); worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils; fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel. turns.message: What is the difference between P0 and P1 codes?
turns.answer:
OBD-II codes have five characters. The letter shows the system: P for powertrain, B for body, C for chassis and U for network. P0 and P2 codes are generic, P1 codes are manufacturer-specific, and P3 codes are split between generic and manufacturer-specific.

For P0 codes the third character shows the area: 1 and 2 fuel and air metering, 3 ignition and misfire, 4 emissions controls, 5 speed and idle control, 6 computer and outputs, 7 and 8 transmission.

turns.message: What should I check before renting a car?

turns.message: It squeals when I brake
turns.answer:
A squeak or squeal when braking is usually caused by the pads and rotors: worn pads touching their wear indicator, moisture or light rust, brake dust, or glazed friction surfaces.

Common causes include pads worn down to the wear indicator; moisture or light surface rust, often in the morning or after rain; brake dust or debris between pad and rotor; or glazed pads or rotors.

A brief squeak on the first few stops in damp weather that then goes away is usually moisture. A squeal that is constant or getting louder should be inspected soon.

Grinding or a metal-on-metal sound usually means the pads are worn through; stop driving when it's safe and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: Why is my car overheating?
turns.answer:
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly.

Possible causes include low coolant or a coolant leak; a thermostat stuck closed; a radiator fan that isn't switching on; a failing water pump; or a blocked or damaged radiator.

Once the engine has fully cooled, check the coolant level in the reservoir.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: What about a flat tire?
turns.answer:
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.

Common causes include a nail, screw or other object in the tread; a cut or bulge in the sidewall from a pothole or kerb; a leaking valve; or a poor seal between the tire and the rim.

Use the spare tire or repair kit as the owner's manual describes; a temporary spare has speed and distance limits. If the sidewall is damaged or you can't change it safely, call roadside assistance. In a rental car, contact the rental team first.

turns.message: My steering is heavy
turns.answer:
Steering that suddenly becomes heavy usually means power-steering assistance has been reduced or lost, or a front tire is low.

Common causes include a low or flat front tire; low power-steering fluid or a leak (hydraulic systems); a slipping or broken drive belt; or an electric power-steering fault, often with a warning light.

Check the front tire pressures and look for a flat. Look for a steering warning light on the dashboard.

If steering becomes hard while driving, slow down, hold the wheel firmly and stop somewhere safe. Don't continue if steering is difficult or unpredictable.

turns.message: Is it safe to drive?
turns.answer: Not until it's checked. Heavy steering makes the car harder to control, especially in an emergency, so drive only as far as a safe place and have it inspected.

turns.message: Transmission slipping

Transmission slipping is when the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up as it should, or gears engage late or harshly.

Common causes include low or worn-out transmission fluid; a fluid leak; worn clutches or bands inside the transmission; or a faulty solenoid, sensor or control module.

Note when it slips (cold, hot, a particular gear) and whether a transmission warning light is on. Look for red or brown fluid under the car.

If the car loses drive, the transmission smells burnt or an over-temperature warning appears, stop safely; continuing can cause major damage.

Rapid clicking with dim lights usually points to a weak battery or poor connection; a single click with bright lights can point to the starter. With the engine off, check that the battery terminals are tight and free of corrosion.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

Note when it happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether the check-engine light is on or flashing. Have the diagnostic codes read; a cylinder-specific code such as P0301 shows where to start.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the car loses power, slow down and stop somewhere safe; a severe misfire can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.
